before: When a file is run as the top-level program, its __name__ is "__main__". When imported normally as greeting_tool, its __name__ is "greeting_tool". These are strings set by the execution context, not names you should manually overwrite.

Place this main.py beside greeting_tool.py:
```python
import greeting_tool
print(greeting_tool.greeting("Ada"))
```
It prints only Hello Ada. Import makes the definitions available but the guard skips the demonstration. Running python greeting_tool.py directly prints Hello Reader instead. Import still executes other unguarded top-level statements; the guard is not a blanket no-side-effects guarantee.

```python
import greeting_tool
greeting_tool.main()
```
It prints Hello Reader because you explicitly called main. The guard controls an automatic call during loading, not whether main may ever be called. This two-file example needs the supplied companion file; a single pasted import cannot create it.

Here is a complete wrapper call using the same companion:
```python
import greeting_tool
def personal_greeting(name):
    return greeting_tool.greeting(name)
print(personal_greeting("Ada"))
```
It prints Hello Ada. In the editor, complete the main-program caller: import the supplied greeting_tool and define personal_greeting(name) to return greeting_tool.greeting(name). Do not print or call main during this import/use exercise. Native and browser fixtures separately check the companion’s guarded behavior. Optional local transfer: run the companion directly, then run the importing main.py and compare the output.
